appraisal_events.evidence: Gilberte turns her face away "d'un air indifférent et dédaigneux", lets her gaze pass over him "sans avoir l'air de me voir" with a hidden smile and an "geste indécent" the boy can only read, by his "petit dictionnaire de civilité", as "outrageant mépris" and "intention insolente"; the name Gilberte then opens onto "l'inconnu de sa vie où je n'entrerais pas".
appraisal_events.explanation: The dominant local movement is a snub that leaves the narrator humiliated and shut out of Gilberte's world; the narration ironizes the reading itself by attributing the verdict of contempt to the child's schoolroom code of manners rather than confirming it.

appraisal_events.evidence: The mother's "voix perçante et autoritaire" calls her away and she obeys "sans qu'elle répliquât", "d'un air docile"; the narrator notes this showed her "comme forcée d'obéir à quelqu'un, comme n'étant pas supérieure à tout", which "calma un peu ma souffrance" and "diminua mon amour".
appraisal_events.explanation: A second, clearly separate moment lowers Gilberte from the sovereign figure of the snub to a child under command, and the narrator explicitly draws that conclusion and registers its effect on his feeling.

appraisal_events.evidence: "Ce pauvre Swann, quel rôle ils lui font jouer : on le fait partir pour qu'elle reste seule avec son Charlus, car c'est lui, je l'ai reconnu ! Et cette petite, mêlée à toute cette infamie !"
appraisal_events.explanation: The grandfather's aside pities and lowers Swann through his wife's arrangement with Charlus, making him a man manipulated inside a household described as infamous; the narration reports the remark without endorsing or undercutting it.

appraisal_events.evidence: She promises to drive to the park gate and means it sincerely, but "le désir qu'elle en avait suffisait à ce qui lui restait de forces"; the narrator names "ce grand renoncement de la vieillesse qui se prépare à la mort" and states she must have known "qu'elle ne reverrait pas Swann, qu'elle ne quitterait plus jamais la maison".
appraisal_events.explanation: The closing paragraph narrates Léonie's definitive withdrawal from the outside world, her door already shut to everyone and now shut even to the one visitor she still asked for; the narrator's own framing carries the judgment.

status_effects.explanation: He is left supplicating, humiliated, and wishing he could have hurt her in return; all the leverage in the encounter lies with Gilberte.

The passage draws an explicit boundary around Gilberte's life — the intimacy of "les êtres heureux qui vivaient, qui voyageaient avec elle" — and places him outside it, in "l'inconnu de sa vie où je n'entrerais pas".
Her indifference and unreadable smile give her complete emotional command over a boy who cannot make her notice him.
At the later moment of the mother's command she is shown as subordinate rather than sovereign, and the narrator's love and her hold on him measurably slacken.
He is pitied aloud as a man given a humiliating role in his own household's arrangements.
She crosses definitively to the inside of her own reclusion: the last visits she received are past, she will not see Swann again, and she will never leave the house.

ambiguities: Gilberte's gesture and fixed look are read as "outrageant mépris" only through the child's "petit dictionnaire de civilité"; the narration marks that reading as the boy's and leaves the gesture's actual intent open, so the snub's polarity is certain for the narrator's experience but not for Gilberte's meaning.
The "dame en blanc" is unnamed in the passage; she is taken as Odette on the strength of "la mère de Gilberte" and the grandfather's remark about Swann's household.
